docs.title: academicflow
docs.text:
Write, check, cite and export scientific papers without leaving Jupyter.

pip install academicflow

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Text analysis: word count, reading time, readability grade, keywords, passive voice.
  • Style checker: informal language, repeated phrases, and section-aware rules such as tense in Methods and abstract length.
  • Terminology consistency: catches "data set" vs "dataset" and undefined acronyms across the whole paper.
  • Venue profiles: apa, ieee and nature presets control citation format, word limits and style rules together.
  • Citations: load a .bib file, write [@key], and get APA, IEEE or Nature formatting, plus checks for missing keys and duplicate DOIs.
  • Abstract generator: extractive by default, with an optional LLM backend.
  • Export: one command to .docx or .tex, with references already formatted.

docs.title: How it differs from existing tools
docs.text: Tool Does academicflow adds textstat Readability scores Section-aware rules, notebook integration proselint Generic prose linting Academic and venue-specific rules, cross-section terminology pybtex BibTeX parsing Inline citation rendering in notebooks, integrity checks nbconvert Notebook conversion Paper-structured export with formatted references

docs.title: Text analysis (academicflow.core)
docs.text:
The core module turns raw text (plain or Markdown) into numbers and highlights: sentences, tokens, readability, keywords and passive voice. It needs no internet, no API key and no downloaded data.

from academicflow.core import analyze, detect_passive

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Function What it does split_sentences(text) Returns (start, end) character offsets of each sentence. tokenize(text) Returns lowercase word tokens. strip_markdown(text) Removes Markdown, code and LaTeX syntax. count_syllables(word) Estimates syllables in one word. readability(text) Flesch Reading Ease and Flesch-Kincaid Grade. basic_counts(text) Word count, sentence count, average sentence length, reading time. extract_keywords(text, top_n=10) RAKE-style keyword phrases, scores 0-1. detect_passive(text) Passive-voice constructions as Issue objects. passive_ratio(text) Share of sentences that contain a passive construction. analyze(text) Everything above in one TextStats.

docs.title: Sentences and tokens
docs.text:
split_sentences does not split after e.g., i.e., et al., Fig., Eq., Dr., vs., inside decimals such as 3.14, or inside [@key] citations. Headings and blank lines always end a sentence.

>>> t = "We did this, e.g. twice. It worked."
>>> [t[s:e] for s, e in split_sentences(t)]
['We did this, e.g. twice.', 'It worked.']
>>> tokenize("COVID-19 results [@smith2020] improved.")
['covid-19', 'results', 'improved']

Hyphenated words and words with digits stay whole. Citations, Markdown syntax, inline code and $...$ math are ignored when counting.

docs.title: Readability
docs.text:
>>> readability("The cat sat on the mat.")["flesch_kincaid_grade"]
-1.45

Both formulas are the standard Flesch formulas. Syllables are counted with a heuristic (vowel groups, silent final e, -le endings, small exceptions table). Reading time uses 238 words per minute.

docs.title: Keywords
docs.text:
Keywords are scored with RAKE: the text is split into phrases (1-3 words) at stopwords and punctuation, and each phrase is scored from its words. Scores are normalised so the best phrase is 1.0. The result is deterministic.

>>> extract_keywords("Deep learning is a method. Deep learning is useful.", 1)
[('deep learning', 1.0)]

docs.title: Passive voice
docs.text:
A form of "to be" (optionally after has/have/will/can..., optionally followed by an adverb) plus a past participle (regular -ed or a bundled list of irregular participles). If spaCy and en_core_web_sm are installed, dependency labels are used instead. This is detected automatically and falls back silently.

>>> issue = detect_passive("The samples were analysed.")[0]
>>> issue.message
'Passive voice: "were analysed".'
>>> (issue.start, issue.end)
(12, 25)

start and end are offsets in the text you passed in, so they can be used for highlighting.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
>>> t = ("Transformers changed NLP [@vaswani2017]. The models were trained on large corpora. "
...      "It has been shown that attention improves translation quality. "
...      "We evaluated the results on three benchmarks.")
>>> analyze(t)
TextStats(word_count=26, sentence_count=4, reading_time_min=0.1092436974789916,
flesch_reading_ease=60.32, flesch_kincaid_grade=6.46, avg_sentence_length=6.5,
keywords=[('attention improves translation', 1.0), ('transformers changed nlp', 1.0),
('large corpora', 0.4444), ('three benchmarks', 0.4444), ('evaluated', 0.1111),
('models', 0.1111), ('quality', 0.1111), ('trained', 0.1111)], passive_ratio=0.5)

docs.title: Empty input
docs.text: Every function accepts an empty string and returns zeros or an empty list.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Passive voice: adjectival participles ("is interested", "was located") are flagged as passive. Participles shorter than 5 letters ending in -ed are only found if they are in the irregular list. Passive detection with spaCy is more accurate but optional.
  • Keywords: there is no part-of-speech tagging, so verbs can appear inside key phrases ("improves translation"). Single words that occur once score low.
  • Long phrases: phrases longer than 3 words are cut into chunks, so a term like "optional large language model" can appear as "optional large language".
  • Sentences: a single capital letter followed by a dot is treated as an initial (J. Smith), so Plan B. We ... is not split.
  • Headings: Markdown heading lines count as one sentence each.
  • Syllables: a heuristic, not a dictionary. Rare words can be off by one, which moves the readability scores slightly.
  • English only.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
One command turns the notebook session into a finished manuscript with formatted citations and a reference list.

%aexport paper.docx     # Word
%aexport paper.tex      # LaTeX
%aexport paper.md       # Markdown

Or from Python:

from academicflow.export import export_document, export_notebook
from academicflow.magics.session import get_session

export_document(get_session(), "paper.docx", fmt="docx")   # "docx" | "latex" | "md"

docs.title: What the document contains
docs.text:
1. Title and authors (if set with %%academic --title)
  2. Abstract (from %aabstract or an abstract section)
  3. Sections in the order you wrote them, each with a heading
  4. A References list in the chosen style

Sections named section-<n> (the automatic names) get no heading.

Citations are rendered in one pass over the whole paper, so IEEE and Nature number references in order of first appearance across all sections.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
DOCX. Built with pypandoc (bundled pandoc). The reference document sets Times New Roman, 12 pt, 1.5 line spacing. To use your own styles, place a reference.docx in academicflow/export/templates/. If pandoc fails, a simpler python-docx version is written and a warning is shown.

LaTeX. The body is converted with pandoc and placed in templates/article.tex (article class, title, author, abstract environment, sections). APA gets a hanging-indent reference section, IEEE and Nature get thebibliography. The .tex file is written without TeX installed, and compiles with pdflatex.

Markdown. Plain markdown. Nature citations use <sup>n</sup>.

docs.title: Export without Jupyter
docs.text:
from academicflow.export import export_notebook

export_notebook("paper.ipynb", "paper.docx", fmt="docx", style="apa", bib_path="refs.bib")

or from a terminal:

python -m academicflow.export paper.ipynb paper.docx --style=ieee --bib refs.bib

The notebook is read like this:

  • Cells starting with %%academic are used. --section, --title, --authors and --style are honoured.
  • If there are none, all markdown cells are used: the first # Heading is the title and ## headings name the sections.
  • The bibliography is bib_path, or the first %acite PATH found in the notebook.
  • A style argument other than "apa" overrides --style in the cells.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• The pandoc-based DOCX uses pandoc's styles for headings and the title block, adjusted to Times New Roman. Journal-specific templates need a custom reference.docx.
  • Figures and tables in cells are passed through pandoc but are not specially numbered.
  • The python-docx fallback supports bold, italic and superscripts only.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: The exported Word file:

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install academicflow

Optional extras: pip install "academicflow[llm]" for LLM abstracts, "academicflow[nlp]" for spaCy-based analysis.

docs.title: Five-minute tour
docs.text:
%load_ext academicflow
%acite refs.bib

%%academic --style=apa --section=introduction
Large language models have changed NLP [@vaswani2017].

%astats
%acheck
%aabstract
%aexport paper.docx

docs.title: Jupyter magics
docs.text:
academicflow adds six magics that turn a notebook into a paper-writing workspace. They keep one shared session (venue profile, bibliography, sections, title, authors, abstract) and call the other modules: core, style, cite, summarize and export.

%load_ext academicflow
Magic What it does %acite refs.bib Load a BibTeX file into the session %%academic Render, store and check one section %astats [section] Statistics table, keywords, highlighted passive voice %acheck Whole-document style check + citation integrity %aabstract [--words=200] [--llm] Generate and store the abstract %aexport paper.docx Export to DOCX, LaTeX or Markdown

Every magic accepts --debug. Without it, errors appear as a short red message instead of a traceback.

docs.title: %acite
docs.text:
%acite refs.bib
# Loaded 12 references from refs.bib

docs.title: %%academic
docs.text:
%%academic --style=apa --section=introduction
Transformers [@vaswani2017] changed machine translation.

Options:

  • --style=apa|ieee|nature (or a path to a custom profile YAML) sets the venue profile for the whole session. It persists for later cells.
  • --section=NAME names the section. Without it the cell is called section-<n>.
  • --no-check hides the style-issue panel.
  • --title marks the cell as the title block (see below).

The cell output shows the text with formatted citations, the references cited in this cell, and a collapsible panel of style issues with severity colours. Re-running a cell with the same --section replaces the section and keeps its position. Auto-named cells are matched by their exact text, so give edited cells a --section name.

If the text has [@key] citations and no bibliography is loaded, a hint asks you to run %acite.

Title and authors:

%%academic --title
Effects of Sleep on Memory
Ada Lovelace
Alan Turing

The first line is the title, each further line is one author. --authors="A; B" also works.

Note

Numbered styles (IEEE, Nature) number references per cell in the cell output. The exported document numbers them across the whole paper, by order of first appearance.

docs.title: %astats
docs.text: %astats introduction shows the statistics for one section. %astats alone covers the whole document (without the abstract). The output has word count, sentence count, reading time, readability scores, average sentence length, passive ratio, top keywords and the text with passive-voice phrases highlighted.

docs.title: %acheck
docs.text:
Runs style.check_document for the stored sections and cite.check_integrity for the full text. Issues are grouped by section with counts per severity. Citation problems are assigned to the section where the citation occurs. Problems without a position (for example an unused bibliography entry) appear under Document / bibliography. A clean paper prints "No issues found".

Switching --style=apa to --style=nature in a later %%academic cell changes which rules and limits apply to the next %acheck.

docs.title: %aabstract
docs.text: Builds the abstract from all sections except abstract and stores it as session.abstract and as the abstract section. --words sets the maximum length. --llm uses the optional LLM backend and falls back to the extractive summarizer when it is unavailable.

docs.title: %aexport
docs.text:
%aexport paper.docx
%aexport paper.tex
%aexport notes.md --format=md

The format comes from the extension unless --format is given. The magic prints the absolute path and shows a download link. See Export.

docs.title: Session API
docs.text:
from academicflow.magics.session import get_session, reset_session

session = get_session()
session.sections      # ordered dict: name -> markdown
reset_session()       # start a new paper

docs.title: Style checker and venue profiles
docs.text:
academicflow.style reviews academic prose at three levels: individual wording, section-specific expectations, and consistency across an entire multi-section paper.

The checks are deterministic, work offline, and do not require NLTK, spaCy, an LLM, or any model download. They are heuristic writing aids rather than substitutes for the target journal's current author instructions or a human editor. In particular, verb-tense detection and acronym recognition are intentionally rule-based and can produce false positives or miss unusual constructions.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
from academicflow.style import check, check_document, load_profile

profile = load_profile("nature")
print(profile["abstract_max_words"])  # 200

issues = check(
    "We use a lot of data in this study.",
    profile="apa",
    section="2. Methods",
)
for issue in issues:
    print(issue.rule, issue.message, issue.suggestion)

paper = {
    "Introduction": "The dataset contains public records.",
    "Methods": "The data set was filtered before analysis.",
}
for issue in check_document(paper, profile="apa"):
    print(issue.section, issue.rule, issue.start, issue.end, issue.message)

Each result is an academicflow.types.Issue. start is inclusive and end is exclusive; both are character offsets into the original text of the reported section.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
Rule ID What it flags Severity Profile-dependent informal-word Informal or imprecise words and phrases from the bundled YAML dictionary warning No contraction English contractions such as don't and isn't warning Yes: allow_contractions first-person I, we, our, or us info Yes: allow_first_person long-sentence Sentence exceeding max_sentence_words warning Yes repeated-word Adjacent duplicate words such as the the warning No repeated-phrase A repeated 3–5-word phrase used at least three times warning No weasel-word Vague emphasis or hedge expressions such as obviously and very info No abstract-length Abstract longer than the configured word limit warning Yes: abstract_max_words / section setting citation-in-abstract Pandoc-style [@key] citation in an abstract that forbids citations warning Yes tense-inconsistency Recognisable present-tense patterns in a section configured for past tense info Yes term-inconsistency Mixed spelling, hyphenation, spacing, or capitalisation across the document warning Yes: preferred spelling breaks ties acronym-undefined Acronym used before a matching Long Form (LF) definition, or never defined warning No acronym-redefined The same acronym is defined more than once warning No acronym-unused Acronym has fewer than two uses after its definition info No

Rules can be disabled by their IDs using the disabled_rules list in a profile.

docs.title: Built-in profiles
docs.text:
Setting APA-inspired IEEE-inspired Nature-inspired citation_style apa ieee nature allow_first_person true true false allow_contractions false false false max_sentence_words 40 35 35 abstract_max_words 250 250 200 preferred_spelling US US UK Abstract citations discouraged discouraged discouraged Methods / Results tense past heuristic past heuristic past heuristic

These profiles are practical presets for a student project. They are not complete, authoritative reproductions of the APA, IEEE, or Nature editorial manuals. Journals within the same publisher can differ, and the journal's live instructions take priority.

docs.title: Section-aware checks
docs.text:
Section headings are case-insensitive, numbered prefixes are removed, and common synonyms are normalised. For example:

  • 2. Methods, Methodology, and Materials and Methods become methods.
  • Summary becomes abstract.
  • Conclusions and Concluding Remarks become conclusion.
  • Discussion remains distinct from Conclusion.

The abstract rule uses the section's max_words when provided, otherwise the profile-level abstract_max_words. Citation checks search for the notebook citation syntax [@key]. Past-tense checks use conservative lexical patterns such as we use and is measured; they are not a full grammatical parser.

docs.title: Cross-document terminology and acronyms
docs.text:
check_document walks sections in insertion order, checks each section individually, then checks the document-wide terminology and acronym state. It currently recognises common space/hyphen/joined variants (including data set, data-set, and dataset), more than 80 US/UK spelling pairs, and mid-sentence lower/title-case variants.

Acronym definitions are recognised in the form Long Form (LF). Connecting words such as of, and, the, and for are ignored when matching initials. Acronym checks are deliberately simple: unusual abbreviations, pluralised acronyms, or long forms with non-standard initials may need manual review.

docs.title: Custom profile
docs.text:
Create a YAML file, for example my-journal.yaml:

name: my-journal
citation_style: apa
allow_first_person: false
allow_contractions: false
max_sentence_words: 32
abstract_max_words: 180
preferred_spelling: uk
disabled_rules:
  - weasel-word
section_rules:
  abstract:
    max_words: 180
    forbid_citations: true
  methods:
    tense: past
  results:
    tense: past
  discussion:
    tense: any

Load it by path:

profile = load_profile("my-journal.yaml")
issues = check(text, profile="my-journal.yaml", section="Methods")

Supported top-level keys are name, citation_style, allow_first_person, allow_contractions, max_sentence_words, abstract_max_words, section_rules, preferred_spelling, and disabled_rules. Section settings support max_words, forbid_citations, and tense (past or any). Missing values are filled from the defaults; unknown or invalid values raise a descriptive ValueError.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
For:

We use a lot of data. The dataset was really big. The the results are shown.

A typical APA-inspired check can report:

informal-word    'a lot of' and 'big'
repeated-word    second occurrence of 'the'
weasel-word      'really'

Actual issue offsets always refer to the exact input string. Suggested replacements are not applied automatically: context determines the academically appropriate wording.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Informal-word and hedge dictionaries are English-language heuristics.
  • Sentence splitting and tokenisation are delegated to academicflow.core; their accuracy improves as Member 1's implementation matures.
  • Passive/active voice and tense are not inferred with a complete syntactic parser.
  • Cross-document spelling groups are curated, not exhaustive.
  • Acronym matching is based on initials and does not understand every domain-specific convention.
  • A single unusual capitalisation may be intentional (for example, a brand or a software library); review suggestions before changing a manuscript.

docs.title: Abstract generator (academicflow.summarize)
docs.text: Generate a summary of any text, or a full abstract from a paper's sections. The default method is extractive TextRank: it runs offline, needs no API key and gives the same result every time. An optional LLM backend writes new sentences instead, and falls back to TextRank automatically if anything goes wrong.

docs.title: In a notebook
docs.text:
%load_ext academicflow

%%academic --section=introduction
...

%aabstract              # TextRank abstract, 200 words
%aabstract --words=150  # shorter
%aabstract --llm        # LLM abstract (see configuration below)

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
from academicflow.summarize import summarize, generate_abstract

summarize(long_text, max_words=100)

generate_abstract({
    "1. Introduction": "...",
    "2. Materials and Methods": "...",
    "Results": "...",
    "Conclusion": "...",
}, max_words=200)

docs.title: How the extractive method works
docs.text:
1. The text is split into sentences, and each sentence becomes a TF-IDF vector (stopwords removed).
  2. Sentences are linked by cosine similarity, and PageRank scores how central each sentence is.
  3. Sentences in the first or last 20% of the text get a small boost (×1.15), as do sentences containing the text's top keywords (×1.10).
  4. The best sentences that fit in max_words are returned in their original order.

generate_abstract is section-aware. It takes up to two of the best sentences from the introduction, methods, results and conclusion, in that order, and shares the word budget between the sections that exist. Section names are normalised:

You write Treated as Introduction, Background, Motivation introduction Methods, Methodology, Materials and Methods, Approach, Experiments methods Results, Evaluation, Findings results Conclusion, Discussion, Summary, Future work conclusion

Numbering such as 2. or III. is ignored, and any existing Abstract section is skipped. If none of the four standard sections exist, the whole text is summarised.

docs.title: LLM backend (optional)
docs.text:
pip install "academicflow[llm]"

Any OpenAI-compatible API works. Configure it with environment variables or with arguments (model=, base_url=, api_key=):

Variable Meaning Example ACADEMICFLOW_LLM_MODEL Model name (required) llama3.2 ACADEMICFLOW_LLM_BASE_URL API URL; leave unset for OpenAI http://localhost:11434/v1 OPENAI_API_KEY API key; not needed for local servers

Local and free, with Ollama:

ollama pull llama3.2
export ACADEMICFLOW_LLM_MODEL=llama3.2
export ACADEMICFLOW_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1

summarize(text, method="llm")
generate_abstract(sections, method="llm")

The model is told to use only facts from the text and never to invent results or citations. Answers longer than max_words are cut at a sentence boundary.

If the openai package, the model name or the key is missing, or the request fails, you get one warning and the TextRank result instead, so a demo never breaks.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Extractive summaries reuse the author's sentences, so they can read less smoothly than a hand-written abstract.
  • Sentence splitting quality depends on academicflow.core.split_sentences.
  • LLM output should always be checked by the authors before submission.
